## 📄 2-Page Analytical Summary — Highlights

### PAGE 1 — Key Cultural Factors (7 Identified)

| # | Cultural Factor | Core Dynamic |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Kinship & Peer Apprenticeship** | Learning via trusted social bonds, not formal teachers |
| 2 | **Oral Transmission & Storytelling** | Narratives as the primary knowledge-transfer vehicle |
| 3 | **Collective Practice > Private Study** | Group participation precedes individual competence |
| 4 | **Elder Authority Structures** | Socially regulated gatekeeping of teaching roles |
| 5 | **Multilingual Flexibility** | Code-switching as adaptive, socially modeled behavior |
| 6 | **Learning in Everyday Responsibilities** | No separation between living and learning |
| 7 | **Community-Driven Motivation** | Collective reputation over individual achievement |

---

### PAGE 2 — Theoretical Comparisons

| Theory | Alignment | Key Tension / Insight |
|---|---|---|
| **Situated Learning** (Lave & Wenger) | ⭐ Very Strong | Authentic context-bound activity throughout |
| **Communities of Practice** (Wenger) | ⭐ Very Strong | Peripheral → full participation mirrors apprenticeship model exactly |
| **Social Learning Theory** (Bandura) | ⭐ Strong | Observation, imitation & social feedback visible in all activities |
| **Dialogic/Experiential Ed** (Dewey, Freire) | ✅ Moderate-Strong | Tension: authority hierarchies conflict with Freire's horizontal dialogue ideal |
| **Self-Determination Theory** (Deci & Ryan) | ⚠️ Partial | Relatedness is central; *individual autonomy* dimension may be culturally limited |

### 🔑 Central Insight
> **Legitimacy in learning is culturally granted** — not meritocratic. Age, kinship trust, and demonstrated community contribution determine who may teach, not pedagogical certification alone. This finding challenges universalist assumptions in several mainstream informal education theories.
